title: Revisiting Triplet Contrastive Learning for 3D Shape Understanding

paper.title: Revisiting Triplet Contrastive Learning for 3D Shape Understanding
paper.abstract: Abstract In multi-modal 3D pre-training, aligning 3D shapes, their 2D image counterparts, and language descriptions has made tremendous progress. However, we find that supervision from rendered images is unreliable, the semantics encoded in synthetic views are distorted due to domain gap, self-occlusion, and rendering artifacts. Instead, we learn transferable 3D representations from language only. We observe that, in real world, 3D shapes are organized in a tree-like structure, ranging from general concepts to fine-grained instances with specific attributes, while language typically denotes generic concepts and subsumes these various 3D instantiations. Hence, we propose to embed 3D representations in hyperbolic space, whose geometry is well-suited for modeling tree-like data without distortion. To capture the asymmetric hierarchy between language and 3D shapes, we further impose a partial-order relation that language entails 3D shapes. Our method, Hyper bolic C ontrastive L earning (HyperCL), jointly optimizes a hyperbolic geodesic-based contrastive objective and an entailment loss to learn discriminative cross-modal representations while explicitly preserving this hierarchy. We also introduce a rigorously verified benchmark for comprehensively evaluating cross-modal 3D alignment. Across two widely used benchmarks and ours, we improve the performance up to 4.6% absolute percentage on 3D shape classification and 5.5% on cross-modal text-to-3D retrieval under the same parameter budget. The code and evaluation benchmark will be made publicly available.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Triplet contrastive learning. Multi-modal 3D contrastive pre-training ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Xue et al., 2023 ; Xue et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2024b ) has emerged as a predominant paradigm for learning transferable 3D representations across various downstream tasks, e.g. , zero-shot point cloud classification and cross-modal shape retrieval. However, unlike web-scale image-text data used to pretrain 2D vision-language models ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , high-quality language annotations for 3D shapes are extremely scarce. As a result, rendered images are often used as visual proxies for generating synthetic captions via image captioning models ( Li et al., 2023 ; Achiam et al., 2023 ) . Given these tri-modal triplets, existing methods align 3D shapes bidirectionally with language descriptions and rendered images in a shared semantic space. While this triplet contrastive learning paradigm substantially alleviates the need for manually labeled 3D annotations, it has several limitations. Rendered images exhibit a severe domain gap w.r.t. natural images used to pretrain 2D vision-language models, i.e. , shifted foreground color statistics and large blank background areas ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) . Furthermore, manually positioned virtual cameras following a predefined trajectory cause severe self-occlusion in certain perspectives during rendering ( Luo et al., 2024 ) . The rendering pipeline itself could also introduce unexpected errors, such as color distortions and complete rendering failures. Consequently, learning from these incomplete and misleading semantics in rendered images inevitably has a negative impact on the alignment. Zhang et al. (2024) attempts to address the unreliable image supervision by first adapting CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) image encoder to rendered 3D views, thereby reducing the domain gap. However, how to avoid self-occlusion that fundamentally distorts the perceived 3D shape semantics still remains an open problem. For example, even a person may mistake a living room viewed behind its exterior wall for a rectangular box. Hence we advocate learning from language supervisions only to reduce the influence of low-fidelity and unreliable semantics in vision modality. Hyperbolic representation learning. In the real world, 3D shapes often convey multifaceted semantics, ranging from various categories to intricate details like color, texture, geometry, design style, and functionality. This naturally organizes into a coarse-to-fine-grained tree that spans a wide spectrum of semantic granularities. In this hierarchy, general concepts described by language are typically positioned near the root, whereas leaf nodes represent specific 3D instantiations characterized by unique attributes. Existing approaches mainly use Euclidean space to model this tree-like structure. However, Euclidean space often struggles to preserve the underlying hierarchical structure without distortion due to its limited polynomial volume growth. As the depth of the underlying tree increases, many fine-grained concepts are compressed into a small region in the space, leading to reduced discriminative capacity. This limitation is particularly prominent in 3D shape understanding, where many real-world instances share a common coarse semantic but differ in subtle attributes. In contrast, hyperbolic space is naturally suitable for tree-like data that has exponential volume growth w.r.t. its radius. This geometric property makes it useful to model an exponentially branching tree without losing discrimination capacity. Hence we propose to contrast 3D shapes against languages in hyperbolic space using a novel hyperbolic contrastive objective. The hyperbolic geometry also allows us to model the asymmetric relation between language and 3D shapes, i.e. , language entails 3D shapes. To encode it explicitly, we further propose an entailment loss that ensures positive 3D representations lie inside the entailment cone of its paired text, and negative 3D shapes outside the cone. Experimental results demonstrate superior performance of our HyperCL on both zero-shot 3D shape recognition and cross-modal retrieval, enabling fine-grained cross-modal discrimination while preserving the vision-language hierarchy embedded in data. Overall, our contributions are summarized as the following: - We identify the limitations of existing triplet contrastive learning framework, and propose to learn from language supervision only. - We introduce HyperCL, a novel approach leveraging hyperbolic geometry to model the tree-like structure embedded in 3D data and enforce a partial-order relation in which language entails 3D shapes, enhancing fine-grained discrimination while preserving the hierarchy. - We create a high-quality, manually verified benchmark to rigorously evaluate 3D cross-modal alignment. Experiments show that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art by a large margin on 3D shape classification, text-to-3D, and 3D-to-text retrieval tasks.

sections.heading: 2.1 3D Triplet Contrastive Learning
sections.text: Multi-modal 3D pre-training has made tremendous progress in recent years. Besides learning from natural language supervision via bi-directional contrastive loss, the point cloud encoder also contrasts with rendered images of 3D shapes, forming a triplet of (point cloud, text, image). Due to the fact that 3D captioning is underexplored, pioneering works Liu et al. (2023) ; Xue et al. (2023) ; Xue et al. (2024) ; Luo et al. (2023) ; Luo et al. (2024) focus on how to accurately describe 3D shapes. They first render 3D shapes from preset viewpoints using Blender, then prompt pre-trained image captioning models ( Achiam et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2023 ) to generate language descriptions. To cope with the scarcity of 3D pre-training data, Uni3D Zhou et al. (2024) initializes its point cloud encoder directly from pretrained 2D image encoders ( Caron et al., 2021 ; Radford et al., 2021 ; Sun et al., 2023 ) instead of training from scratch, establishing a strong optimization prior. MM-Mixing Wang et al. (2025) mixes different point clouds to learn robust and discriminative representations. MixCon3D Gao et al. (2024b) integrates the distinct yet complementary information between rendered images and point clouds to contrast with languages. MRD Wang et al. (2024) performs multi-modal distillation to maintain the semantic relations of both intra- and inter-modalities in the embedding space. However, given rendered images, CLIP fails to encode meaningful semantics from rendered images due to domain gap. Besides, how to position virtual cameras and select appropriate viewpoints to avoid self-occlusion is still an open problem. Furthermore, rendering pipeline sometimes leads to unexpected errors. TAMM Zhang et al. (2024) adds an extra stage that adapts CLIP image encoder via adapter ( Gao et al., 2024a ) to rendered images for extracting faithful semantic information. However, better alignment with rendered images during training does not necessarily translate into better generalization, possibly due to overlapped semantics with language. Even if the distorted semantics brought by domain gap can be faithfully restored, the multi-view rendering at scale is prohibitively expensive, and the fundamental self-occlusion issue inherent to any 2D projection of 3D shapes remains difficult to address. Hence we propose to learn from language only, bypassing the limitations of the supervision signal in rendered images.

sections.heading: 2.2 Hyperbolic Learning
sections.text: Characterized by the exponential volume expansion, hyperbolic geometry is naturally suited for modeling hierarchical data such as trees and graphs. Hyperbolic learning can be divided into two groups: 1) the first line of work builds hyperbolic neural networks ( Ganea et al., 2018b ; Shimizu et al., 2020 ) by designing hyperbolic counterparts of euclidean layers, such as convolution and multinomial logistic regression, and these networks are optimized using specialized riemannian optimizers; 2) the second group still keeps the main chunk of model in Euclidean space, but with an added exponential mapping projection to transform euclidean features onto hyperbolic data points. Foundational works Nickel and Kiela (2017) ; Nickel and Kiela (2018) establish the efficacy of two representative models in hyperbolic geometry, i.e. , poincaré ball and lorentz model, for capturing lexical hierarchies within text modality. Ganea et al. (2018a) further introduces entailment cone to encode asymmetric is-a relations in hyperbolic space, which inspires our batch-wise entailment loss. In computer vision and multi-modal learning, hyperbolic geometry has been adapted to various tasks including 2D representation learning ( Ermolov et al., 2022 ; Ge et al., 2023 ) , image and emotion classification ( Chen et al., 2023 ; Khrulkov et al., 2020 ; Guo et al., 2022 ) , image segmentation ( Atigh et al., 2022 ) , open-vocabulary perception ( Doan et al., 2024 ; Kong et al., 2024 ; Peng et al., 2025 ) , 2D vision-language models ( Desai et al., 2023 ; Ramasinghe et al., 2024 ; Pal et al., 2025 ) , and scaling models to billions of parameters ( Mandica et al., 2024 ) . However, applying hyperbolic geometry to model 3D data is less explored. Liu et al. (2025) is the first to utilize hyperbolic learning in 3D domain but without large-scale pre-training. Following prior works Desai et al. (2023) ; Kong et al. (2024) that enforce the partial relation such as object entails scenes or caption entails images/objects in 2D, we enforce caption entails 3D shapes to build vision-language hierarchy and adopt the lorentz model which is numerically more stable and suitable for gradient optimization than poincaré ball.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: We first briefly introduce hyperbolic geometry and the triplet contrastive learning paradigm in Section 3.1 . Then we analyze the current pitfall of existing triplet contrastive learning framework in Section 3.2 , followed by our proposed method HyperCL with hyperbolic geodesic-based contrastive loss and entailment loss in Section 3.3 .

sections.heading: 3.3 HyperCL
sections.text: We diagnose whether the learned representation space resembles a tree structure. For this, we choose Uni3D Zhou et al. (2024) , a state-of-the-art model pretrained for 3D understanding. We use δ \delta -hyperbolicity in Khrulkov et al. (2020) ; Fournier et al. (2015) to measure how far the space deviates from a tree, which is zero for a perfect tree and increases as the underlying structure becomes less tree-like (more details are in Appendix A.3 ). As reported in Table 3.2 , the representations induced by euclidean triplet contrastive learning are already intrinsically hierarchical. This reflects the fact that real-world 3D concepts form a vast taxonomy with exponential branching factor. However, the geometry in which these representations are optimized is misaligned with this tree-like structure. Euclidean space only has a polynomial growth with insufficient discrimination capacity. In contrast, hyperbolic space can embed trees without distortion due to its exponential volume growth. Motivated by this, we embed both 3D shapes and language descriptions into hyperbolic space. We next detail our proposed HyperCL with hyperbolic contrastive loss and entailment loss.

sections.heading: 4.1 Implementation Details
sections.text: Following Liu et al. (2023) ; Zhou et al. (2024) , we pretrain on the ensembled dataset including Objaverse Deitke et al. (2023) , ShapeNet Chang et al. (2015) , 3D-FUTURE Fu et al. (2021) , and ABO Collins et al. (2022) . We adopt PointBERT Yu et al. (2022) initialized from EVA02 Fang et al. (2024) with 85.3M trainable parameters as our point cloud encoder unless otherwise noted. EVA02-E-14-plus from EVA Sun et al. (2023) is used as the frozen text encoder. To accelerate training, we precompute text embeddings { 𝐞 ~ T } \{\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}^{T}\} and cache them offline. AdamW Loshchilov and Hutter (2017) with batch size 256 is adopted as the optimizer, and we train for 120 epochs. The final loss is ℒ H = ℒ H P ↔ T + λ ⋅ ℒ H e ​ n ​ t \mathcal{L}_{H}=\mathcal{L}_{H}^{P\leftrightarrow T}+\lambda\cdot\mathcal{L}_{H}^{ent} , where λ \lambda is a balancing factor and set to 0.2. The margin γ \gamma in Equation 8 is set to 0.5. More implementation details and training cost are in the appendix A.1 and A.2 .

sections.heading: 4.2 Evaluation Datasets
sections.text: We adopt two widely used datasets for assessment, including ModelNet40 (MN40) Wu et al. (2015) and Objaverse-LVIS (OLVIS) Deitke et al. (2023) . MN40 is a synthetic CAD model dataset. It contains 2.5K testing samples that span 40 categories. OLVIS is a subset of the Objaverse dataset with human-verified category labels. It has 46K samples spanning 1,156 categories, making it suitable for more challenging open-vocabulary and zero-shot 3D shape classification and retrieval. Our curated benchmark. Astonishingly, despite its manual labeling, many samples in OLVIS are mislabeled, likely due to varied labeling quality. Such noise can lead to misleading conclusions, as it obscures whether a model truly distinguishes fine-grained semantics or simply benefits from annotation artifacts. To obtain a more reliable testbed for cross-modal alignment, we manually verify each 3D shape in OLVIS. Detailed procedures and statistics are listed in appendix A.4 and A.5 . We term the resulting benchmark as cleaned Objaverse-LVIS (c-OLVIS), it contains around 7.7K high-quality samples across 846 categories. c-OLVIS is more trustworthy, by eliminating label noise, it ensures performance gains stem from genuine improvements in 3D semantic understanding rather than fitting to erroneous annotations, while also maintaining a large concept pool to assess real-world 3D understanding.

sections.heading: 4.3 Main Comparison
sections.text: Zero-shot 3D shape classification. We compare with strong baselines under different pre-training data regimes and model parameters in Table 3 . We do not compare with MM-Mixing Wang et al. (2025) , MixCon3D Gao et al. (2024b) , and MRD Wang et al. (2024) as their model weights or codes are not released. When pretrained on ShapeNet containing only 50K objects, we use a smaller model with 21.7M parameters. As shown in Table 3 , our method achieves state-of-the-art performance across all benchmarks under the same parameter budget. Previous best model Uni3D-B achieves 81.6 on our c-OLVIS dataset, whereas we boost the performance to 86.2 with 4.6 absolute improvement. Between a query 3D representation and origin [ROOT] , we interpolate evenly spaced points along the hyperbolic geodesic connecting them, and use each intermediate point to retrieve its nearest category. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we present HyperCL for learning transferable 3D representations. We demonstrate that learning from language supervision only effectively bypasses the inability of VLMs to encode reliable semantics from rendered images. We leverage hyperbolic geometry to enhance discrimination and model the inherent vision-language hierarchy that language entails 3D shapes. The proposed hyperbolic contrastive and batchwise entailment losses effectively preserves this hierarchical structure. Furthermore, our manually verified c-OLVIS benchmark serves as a rigorous evaluation. Experimental results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both 3D shape classification and cross-modal retrieval tasks. Limitations Though the language descriptions are relatively robust than rendered images, the problems caused by self-occlusion and rendering artifacts may still be propagated into captions. 3D captioning is best performed without rendered images as proxy via 3D LLMs that directly take 3D shapes as input. However this is beyond our paper’s scope and we leave this to future work.

sections.text: Gromov hyperbolicity quantifies how closely a metric space resembles the structure of a tree. Let ( ℳ , d ) (\mathcal{M},d) be a metric space, where ℳ \mathcal{M} is the set of representations and d : ℳ × ℳ → ℝ d:\mathcal{M}\times\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is the distance measure. In our experiments, each representation is a 3D shape embedding e ~ i ∈ ℝ D \tilde{e}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} produced by Uni3D ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) , and d d is euclidean metric d ⁡ ( e ~ i , e ~ j ) = ∥ e ~ i − e ~ j ∥ 2 d(\tilde{e}_{i},\tilde{e}_{j})=\lVert\tilde{e}_{i}-\tilde{e}_{j}\rVert_{2} . For a base point e ~ b ∈ ℳ \tilde{e}_{b}\in\mathcal{M} , the Gromov product of e ~ i \tilde{e}_{i} and e ~ j \tilde{e}_{j} is defined as ( e ~ i ∣ e ~ j ) e ~ b = 1 2 ​ ( d ⁡ ( e ~ i , e ~ b ) + d ⁡ ( e ~ j , e ~ b ) − d ⁡ ( e ~ i , e ~ j ) ) . (\tilde{e}_{i}\mid\tilde{e}_{j})_{\tilde{e}_{b}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(d(\tilde{e}_{i},\tilde{e}_{b})+d(\tilde{e}_{j},\tilde{e}_{b})-d(\tilde{e}_{i},\tilde{e}_{j})\right). (9) In a rooted tree, it equals the length of the initial path shared by the paths from e ~ b \tilde{e}_{b} to e ~ i \tilde{e}_{i} and e ~ j \tilde{e}_{j} . Thus, a larger Gromov product indicates a deeper branching point, whereas a smaller value indicates branching closer to the base point. Given three representations e ~ i \tilde{e}_{i} , e ~ j \tilde{e}_{j} , and e ~ k \tilde{e}_{k} , a tree satisfies the following Gromov product inequality: ( e ~ i ∣ e ~ k ) e ~ b ≥ min ⁡ { ( e ~ i ∣ e ~ j ) e ~ b , ( e ~ j ∣ e ~ k ) e ~ b } . (\tilde{e}_{i}\mid\tilde{e}_{k})_{\tilde{e}_{b}}\geq\min\left\{(\tilde{e}_{i}\mid\tilde{e}_{j})_{\tilde{e}_{b}},(\tilde{e}_{j}\mid\tilde{e}_{k})_{\tilde{e}_{b}}\right\}. (10) The deviation from this tree condition is quantified by the base-point Gromov hyperbolicity: δ e ~ b = max e ~ i , e ~ j , e ~ k ∈ ℳ ⁡ [ min ⁡ { ( e ~ i ∣ e ~ j ) e ~ b , ( e ~ j ∣ e ~ k ) e ~ b } − ( e ~ i ∣ e ~ k ) e ~ b ] . \delta_{\tilde{e}_{b}}=\max_{\tilde{e}_{i},\tilde{e}_{j},\tilde{e}_{k}\in\mathcal{M}}\left[\min\left\{(\tilde{e}_{i}\mid\tilde{e}_{j})_{\tilde{e}_{b}},(\tilde{e}_{j}\mid\tilde{e}_{k})_{\tilde{e}_{b}}\right\}-(\tilde{e}_{i}\mid\tilde{e}_{k})_{\tilde{e}_{b}}\right]. (11) A tree metric has δ e ~ b = 0 \delta_{\tilde{e}_{b}}=0 , since the above inequality holds for every triple of points. A positive value measures the largest violation of this condition among sampled representations. Therefore, a smaller value indicates a more tree-like structure, whereas a larger value indicates the opposite. To account for the overall scale of the embedding space, we report the relative hyperbolicity: δ rel = 2 ​ δ e ~ b diam ⁡ ( ℳ ) , diam ⁡ ( ℳ ) = max e ~ i , e ~ j ∈ ℳ ⁡ d ⁡ ( e ~ i , e ~ j ) . \delta_{\mathrm{rel}}=\frac{2\delta_{\tilde{e}_{b}}}{\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{M})},\qquad\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{M})=\max_{\tilde{e}_{i},\tilde{e}_{j}\in\mathcal{M}}d(\tilde{e}_{i},\tilde{e}_{j}). sections.heading: A.4 More Details on c-OLVIS Construction
sections.text: Figure 6: Examples from the manual verification. For four categories lollipop, birdhouse, combination_lock and turkey_(food), the upper row shows 3D shapes that were correctly labelled and kept in our c-OLVIS, while the lower row shows OLVIS samples that were mislabelled and removed. Based on OLVIS, we construct a cleaned version of it through manual inspection and refinement. During inspection, for each object we utilize the official Sketchfab website stored in the metadata. The viewer supports rotation and zooming in of the 3D shape, allowing labelers to inspect it from multiple viewpoints and reduce errors caused by self-occlusion. To ensure consistent criteria, each 3D shape will display its assigned category name, associated synonyms, along with its LVIS definition. This information helps reviewers distinguish intended category from polysemy. We develop a lightweight annotation tool that provides three possible options: accepted (a), rejected (r), and unsure (u). Annotators can submit decision by pressing corresponding key, and the tool automatically opens the online URL using chromium. We evenly split OLVIS into three disjoint subsets and assign each subset to one labeler. Candidates marked as accepted during initial screening phase are passed for a second round of review by other independent labelers. Only candidates accepted in both stages are kept in our c-OLVIS benchmark. This two stage procedure reduces the chances that an individual oversight or inconsistent interpretation propagates into the final benchmark. We encourage annotators to label it as unsure rather than accepted to avoid being deterministically filtered out in second round. Objects marked as unsure in the first round are collected and sent for committee screening as detailed next. We find that many categories in OLVIS are either intrinsically ambiguous or related with each other via parent-child and synonym relationships. For example, table is the parent concept of dining table and coffee table, while in the meantime, it may also be used as a synonym for desk. We first organize such ambiguous concepts into groups via WordNet and instruct reviewers to press unsure button whenever a 3D shape lies in these groups. Then all reviewers are shown the same unsure object, when the group contains parent-children relationship, we apply a strict rule that it should be assigned to the most specific subclass unless it can not be classified into any subclass in that group, then it will be assigned as the parent class. Only the vote for a concept receives more than half of the reviewers then the object will be assigned to that class, otherwise, the object is discarded. We asked three graduate student to independently assess their given split using the same criteria and it takes around 15 days to annotate our c-OLVIS benchmark. The time is mostly spent on waiting for online rendering and committee review for unsure objects. Examples are given in Figure 6 .

sections.heading: A.5 More Statistics of c-OLVIS
sections.text: Figure 7: Statistics of our c-OLVIS. Left: category vocabulary of c-OLVIS, 846 categories in total. Middle: the rank–frequency distribution of class sizes on category-index axis. Right: the number of categories per class-size bin. Compared to OLVIS, c-OLVIS has 7,678 unique 3D shapes from 846 categories, covering 73.2% original categories of OLVIS. This diverse coverage of real-world concepts ensures that our proposed c-OLVIS benchmark remains representative for zero-shot 3D understanding. After rigorous filtering and correction, we remove substantial annotation noise, therefore it provides a more reliable evaluation, allowing the improvement to be more likely to reflect true semantic recognition rather than false exploitation on noisy labels. While at the meantime, even though the accuracy on our c-OLVIS benchmark is typically higher than that on OLVIS, the resulting c-OLVIS benchmark is not merely an easy subset that contains only frequent categories from OLVIS. As shown in Figure 7 , categories that contain less 3D shapes are well preserved, the main annotation noise comes from several categories with a large amount of objects (the rightmost bar in right subfigure). Thus, the large accuracy gap between our c-OLVIS and OLVIS can not be explained simply by retaining a large portion of easily recognizable categories. Instead, it is consistent with our manual verification process that removes many noisy or ambiguous instances while preserving low-frequency concepts. This is exactly why annotation quality matters: a reliable benchmark should reward correct semantic recognition rather than penalize it because of incorrect labels.

However, we find that supervision from rendered images is unreliable, the semantics encoded in synthetic views are distorted due to domain gap, self-occlusion, and rendering artifacts. Instead, we learn transferable 3D representations from language only. We observe that, in real world, 3D shapes are organized in a tree-like structure, ranging from general concepts to fine-grained instances with specific attributes, while language typically denotes generic concepts and subsumes these various 3D instantiations. Hence, we propose to embed 3D representations in hyperbolic space, whose geometry is well-suited for modeling tree-like data without distortion. To capture the asymmetric hierarchy between language and 3D shapes, we further impose a partial-order relation that language entails 3D shapes. Our method, Hyper bolic C ontrastive L earning (HyperCL), jointly optimizes a hyperbolic geodesic-based contrastive objective and an entailment loss to learn discriminative cross-modal representations while explicitly preserving this hierarchy. We also introduce a rigorously verified benchmark for comprehensively evaluating cross-modal 3D alignment. Across two widely used benchmarks and ours, we improve the performance up to 4.6% absolute percentage on 3D shape classification and 5.5% on cross-modal text-to-3D retrieval under the same parameter budget. The code and evaluation benchmark will be made publicly available. 2 2 footnotetext: Corresponding author 1 Introduction Triplet contrastive learning. Multi-modal 3D contrastive pre-training ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Xue et al., 2023 ; Xue et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2024b ) has emerged as a predominant paradigm for learning transferable 3D representations across various downstream tasks, e.g. , zero-shot point cloud classification and cross-modal shape retrieval. However, unlike web-scale image-text data used to pretrain 2D vision-language models ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , high-quality language annotations for 3D shapes are extremely scarce. As a result, rendered images are often used as visual proxies for generating synthetic captions via image captioning models ( Li et al., 2023 ; Achiam et al., 2023 ) . Given these tri-modal triplets, existing methods align 3D shapes bidirectionally with language descriptions and rendered images in a shared semantic space. While this triplet contrastive learning paradigm substantially alleviates the need for manually labeled 3D annotations, it has several limitations. Rendered images exhibit a severe domain gap w.r.t. natural images used to pretrain 2D vision-language models, i.e. , shifted foreground color statistics and large blank background areas ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) . Furthermore, manually positioned virtual cameras following a predefined trajectory cause severe self-occlusion in certain perspectives during rendering ( Luo et al., 2024 ) . The rendering pipeline itself could also introduce unexpected errors, such as color distortions and complete rendering failures. Consequently, learning from these incomplete and misleading semantics in rendered images inevitably has a negative impact on the alignment. Zhang et al. (2024) attempts to address the unreliable image supervision by first adapting CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) image encoder to rendered 3D views, thereby reducing the domain gap. However, how to avoid self-occlusion that fundamentally distorts the perceived 3D shape semantics still remains an open problem. For example, even a person may mistake a living room viewed behind its exterior wall for a rectangular box. Hence we advocate learning from language supervisions only to reduce the influence of low-fidelity and unreliable semantics in vision modality. Hyperbolic representation learning. In the real world, 3D shapes often convey multifaceted semantics, ranging from various categories to intricate details like color, texture, geometry, design style, and functionality. This naturally organizes into a coarse-to-fine-grained tree that spans a wide spectrum of semantic granularities. In this hierarchy, general concepts described by language are typically positioned near the root, whereas leaf nodes represent specific 3D instantiations characterized by unique attributes. Existing approaches mainly use Euclidean space to model this tree-like structure. However, Euclidean space often struggles to preserve the underlying hierarchical structure without distortion due to its limited polynomial volume growth. As the depth of the underlying tree increases, many fine-grained concepts are compressed into a small region in the space, leading to reduced discriminative capacity. This limitation is particularly prominent in 3D shape understanding, where many real-world instances share a common coarse semantic but differ in subtle attributes. In contrast, hyperbolic space is naturally suitable for tree-like data that has exponential volume growth w.r.t. its radius. This geometric property makes it useful to model an exponentially branching tree without losing discrimination capacity. Hence we propose to contrast 3D shapes against languages in hyperbolic space using a novel hyperbolic contrastive objective. The hyperbolic geometry also allows us to model the asymmetric relation between language and 3D shapes, i.e. , language entails 3D shapes. To encode it explicitly, we further propose an entailment loss that ensures positive 3D representations lie inside the entailment cone of its paired text, and negative 3D shapes outside the cone. Experimental results demonstrate superior performance of our HyperCL on both zero-shot 3D shape recognition and cross-modal retrieval, enabling fine-grained cross-modal discrimination while preserving the vision-language hierarchy embedded in data. Overall, our contributions are summarized as the following: - We identify the limitations of existing triplet contrastive learning framework, and propose to learn from language supervision only. - We introduce HyperCL, a novel approach leveraging hyperbolic geometry to model the tree-like structure embedded in 3D data and enforce a partial-order relation in which language entails 3D shapes, enhancing fine-grained discrimination while preserving the hierarchy. - We create a high-quality, manually verified benchmark to rigorously evaluate 3D cross-modal alignment. Experiments show that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art by a large margin on 3D shape classification, text-to-3D, and 3D-to-text retrieval tasks. 2 Related Work 2.1 3D Triplet Contrastive Learning Multi-modal 3D pre-training has made tremendous progress in recent years. Besides learning from natural language supervision via bi-directional contrastive loss, the point cloud encoder also contrasts with rendered images of 3D shapes, forming a triplet of (point cloud, text, image). Due to the fact that 3D captioning is underexplored, pioneering works Liu et al. (2023) ; Xue et al. (2023) ; Xue et al. (2024) ; Luo et al. (2023) ; Luo et al. (2024) focus on how to accurately describe 3D shapes. They first render 3D shapes from preset viewpoints using Blender, then prompt pre-trained image captioning models ( Achiam et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2023 ) to generate language descriptions. To cope with the scarcity of 3D pre-training data, Uni3D Zhou et al. (2024) initializes its point cloud encoder directly from pretrained 2D image encoders ( Caron et al., 2021 ; Radford et al., 2021 ; Sun et al., 2023 ) instead of training from scratch, establishing a strong optimization prior. MM-Mixing Wang et al. (2025) mixes different point clouds to learn robust and discriminative representations. MixCon3D Gao et al. (2024b) integrates the distinct yet complementary information between rendered images and point clouds to contrast with languages. MRD Wang et al. (2024) performs multi-modal distillation to maintain the semantic relations of both intra- and inter-modalities in the embedding space. However, given rendered images, CLIP fails to encode meaningful semantics from rendered images due to domain gap. Besides, how to position virtual cameras and select appropriate viewpoints to avoid self-occlusion is still an open problem. Furthermore, rendering pipeline sometimes leads to unexpected errors. TAMM Zhang et al. (2024) adds an extra stage that adapts CLIP image encoder via adapter ( Gao et al., 2024a ) to rendered images for extracting faithful semantic information. However, better alignment with rendered images during training does not necessarily translate into better generalization, possibly due to overlapped semantics with language. Even if the distorted semantics brought by domain gap can be faithfully restored, the multi-view rendering at scale is prohibitively expensive, and the fundamental self-occlusion issue inherent to any 2D projection of 3D shapes remains difficult to address. Hence we propose to learn from language only, bypassing the limitations of the supervision signal in rendered images. 2.2 Hyperbolic Learning Characterized by the exponential volume expansion, hyperbolic geometry is naturally suited for modeling hierarchical data such as trees and graphs. Hyperbolic learning can be divided into two groups: 1) the first line of work builds hyperbolic neural networks ( Ganea et al., 2018b ; Shimizu et al., 2020 ) by designing hyperbolic counterparts of euclidean layers, such as convolution and multinomial logistic regression, and these networks are optimized using specialized riemannian optimizers; 2) the second group still keeps the main chunk of model in Euclidean space, but with an added exponential mapping projection to transform euclidean features onto hyperbolic data points. Foundational works Nickel and Kiela (2017) ; Nickel and Kiela (2018) establish the efficacy of two representative models in hyperbolic geometry, i.e. , poincaré ball and lorentz model, for capturing lexical hierarchies within text modality. Ganea et al. (2018a) further introduces entailment cone to encode asymmetric is-a relations in hyperbolic space, which inspires our batch-wise entailment loss. In computer vision and multi-modal learning, hyperbolic geometry has been adapted to various tasks including 2D representation learning ( Ermolov et al., 2022 ; Ge et al., 2023 ) , image and emotion classification ( Chen et al., 2023 ; Khrulkov et al., 2020 ; Guo et al., 2022 ) , image segmentation ( Atigh et al., 2022 ) , open-vocabulary perception ( Doan et al., 2024 ; Kong et al., 2024 ; Peng et al., 2025 ) , 2D vision-language models ( Desai et al., 2023 ; Ramasinghe et al., 2024 ; Pal et al., 2025 ) , and scaling models to billions of parameters ( Mandica et al., 2024 ) . However, applying hyperbolic geometry to model 3D data is less explored. Liu et al. (2025) is the first to utilize hyperbolic learning in 3D domain but without large-scale pre-training. Following prior works Desai et al. (2023) ; Kong et al. (2024) that enforce the partial relation such as object entails scenes or caption entails images/objects in 2D, we enforce caption entails 3D shapes to build vision-language hierarchy and adopt the lorentz model which is numerically more stable and suitable for gradient optimization than poincaré ball. 3 Method We first briefly introduce hyperbolic geometry and the triplet contrastive learning paradigm in Section 3.1 . For this, we choose Uni3D Zhou et al. (2024) , a state-of-the-art model pretrained for 3D understanding. We use δ \delta -hyperbolicity in Khrulkov et al. (2020) ; Fournier et al. As reported in Table 3.2 , the representations induced by euclidean triplet contrastive learning are already intrinsically hierarchical. This reflects the fact that real-world 3D concepts form a vast taxonomy with exponential branching factor. However, the geometry in which these representations are optimized is misaligned with this tree-like structure. Euclidean space only has a polynomial growth with insufficient discrimination capacity. In contrast, hyperbolic space can embed trees without distortion due to its exponential volume growth. Motivated by this, we embed both 3D shapes and language descriptions into hyperbolic space. Astonishingly, despite its manual labeling, many samples in OLVIS are mislabeled, likely due to varied labeling quality. (2024) tend to directly jump to [ROOT] , whereas our model yields a much smoother trajectory of meaningful intermediate concepts, revealing multiple levels of abstraction. 5 Conclusion In this paper, we present HyperCL for learning transferable 3D representations. We demonstrate that learning from language supervision only effectively bypasses the inability of VLMs to encode reliable semantics from rendered images. We leverage hyperbolic geometry to enhance discrimination and model the inherent vision-language hierarchy that language entails 3D shapes. The proposed hyperbolic contrastive and batchwise entailment losses effectively preserves this hierarchical structure. Furthermore, our manually verified c-OLVIS benchmark serves as a rigorous evaluation. Experimental results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both 3D shape classification and cross-modal retrieval tasks. Limitations Though the language descriptions are relatively robust than rendered images, the problems caused by self-occlusion and rendering artifacts may still be propagated into captions. 3D captioning is best performed without rendered images as proxy via 3D LLMs that directly take 3D shapes as input. However this is beyond our paper’s scope and we leave this to future work.
